text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed lower in quiet dealings. October closed down $1.30 at $326.0 per tonne, while December ended $1.30 lower at $321.50 per tonne. There was no fresh news to influence trading.

Raw sugar futures in New York ended lower on light commission house selling offset by trade buying at the bottom of the range. The active October contract closed at 11.58 cents/lb, down 7 points from Friday's close. March gave also up 7 points to close at 11.77 cents/lb. Official sources in Thailand confirmed that production will be down in 1997/98, which, however, had no impact on world market prices, as this was generally expected.

However, Thai raw premiums edged up slightly on government forecasts that a dry spell will sharply reduce sugar output for 1997/98. Thai raw sugar premiums for July/September deliveries were quoted around 85-95 points (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange futures on an fob basis, compared with 80-90 earlier last week. January/March deliveries were quoted at 100/120 points per pound over New York, up slightly from last week. Even though world sugar production in 1997/98 is forecast to fall, stocks will remain ample as there seems little chance for a significant pick up in import demand. Hence, the chances for a major rally seem slim unless weather plays havoc with the 1997/98 crop.

THAILAND - Thailand's Cane and Sugar Board estimated 1997/98 cane sugar production at 48.4 million tonnes, down from 56.2 million tonnes produced in 1996/97. Sugar output is expected to fall by nearly 14 percent to 5.02 million tonnes, tel quel, versus 5.82 million tonnes in 1996/97. The board attributed the substantial drop to a severe dry spell which hit various parts of Thailand in April/June.

It was added that the sugar cane in central and eastern regions was hardest hit with 14.6 percent and 18.8 percent respectively of the crops being damaged. About 13.9 percent of sugar cane in the northern area is damaged while the impact of the driest spell in the northeastern region is apparently limited. However, yield is expected to improve marginally in 1997/98 to 10.38 percent from 10.35 per cent in 1996/97, the board said.

SWITZERLAND - Sugar imports in June 1997 amounted to 12,985 tonnes, raw value, down from last year's 13,107 tonnes. This brought cumulative imports in the first three quarters of 1996/97 (October/June) up to 93,261 tonnes against 118,394 tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 169,593 tonnes against 155,620 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in 1996/97 were Germany with 65,027 tonnes whites against 69,424 tonnes and France with 16,073 tonnes, down from 36,204 tonnes.

FRANCE - Sugar imports in May 1997 amounted to 11,479 tonnes, raw value, down from 46,220 tonnes imported in May 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first eight months of 1996/97 (October/May) up to 211,511 tonnes against 352,336 tonnes in 1995/96. Total imports in 1995/96 amounted to 476,587 tonnes compared to 364,140 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in 1996/97 were Belgium-Luxembourg with 35,295 tonnes whites, up from 26,214 tonnes and Germany with 28,135 tonnes compared to 18,470 tonnes.

Sugar exports in May 1997 reached 236,820 tonnes against 186,109 tonnes in May 1996. This brought cumulative exports in October/May 1996/97 up to 1.951 million tonnes against 2.108 million tonnes in 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 amounted to 2.896 million tonnes compared to 3.067 million tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of destination in 1996/97 were Belgium-Luxembourg with 403,314 tonnes whites against 441,774 tonnes, Iran with 232,739 tonnes compared to 158,800 tonnes, Algeria with 152,989 tonnes, up from 42,532 tonnes and Spain with 123,644 tonnes against 139,696 tonnes.
